projects.title: MobiLAB & Care REV app
projects.text:
Problem:

Before the RevApp, doctors and physical therapists would assign exercises to their patients, but progress could only be evaluated through new consultations, making the process inefficient, time-consuming, and costly. The RevApp eliminated these barriers by allowing doctors to remotely track their patients' exercises in real time, improving efficiency, reducing costs, and minimizing unnecessary consultations or patient discomfort.

How it was solved:

The project began with previous Digital Innovation students and their foundation of the RevApp. We were tasked with building upon their work and refining the app to meet the project's goals. One key challenge was connecting the mobile app to a device for tracking patient exercises. After thorough consideration, we decided a mobile app was the best solution, as it could easily interface with a tracking device while also being compatible with doctors' laptops or computers for data access.

The app was built using Flutter, which allowed us to develop the entire app with one unified codebase. However, working with Flutter proved challenging due to its syntax, which made it harder to read and write, presenting a steep learning curve for the team.

One of the technical hurdles was processing the complex data from the Movella Dot sensors, which provided highly accurate but intricate orientation data. The sensors returned quaternion values—sets of four decimal numbers representing an object's orientation relative to Earth. These values were difficult to interpret directly, so we worked closely with our client and conducted extensive research to transform these quaternions into rotation matrices. From there, we could convert them into radians and eventually to a single angle that could be used to track patient movements. This was a pivotal part of the project, as successful angle conversion was crucial for registering exercises and generating usable data.

What I did:

In this project, I was responsible for developing the home page of the doctor's dashboard, where doctors could easily access a list of all their patients and quickly see the four most recent exercises performed. I also worked on data processing—converting quaternion values into readable angles for display in graphs and statistics. Lastly, I helped build the dashboard, allowing doctors to track patient data and view performance stats over time.

One of the most challenging aspects of the project was working with an existing codebase. It took time to familiarize myself with the code before I could begin contributing, but this experience was invaluable in improving my ability to work with larger, more complex systems.

Outcome:

We successfully delivered the app to our client, MobiLab & Care Research Group, and presented our progress in June 2024. The project is still ongoing, and we aim to finalize the first working version by the end of June.

Reflection:

This was my first time working on a large-scale project with a team of more than three people, which was both fun and challenging. The sheer size of the project made communication a bit more difficult, but it was an excellent learning experience in collaboration, technical problem-solving, and project management. Despite the challenges, this project remains one of my favorites due to the technical complexities involved, and it reignited my passion for mathematics and problem-solving.

projects.title: LABflow
projects.text:
Problem:

Biomedical students faced the challenge of using outdated and inefficient paper-based methods for tracking blood samples in their lab exercises. The school couldn't afford the expensive licenses required for commercial lab management software used in real hospitals. This led to the need for a cost-effective, user-friendly system that could mimic real-world laboratory procedures and be used as an educational tool.

How it was solved:

Our team was approached by two teachers to build a Laboratory Information System (LIS) that would help students simulate the process of blood sample handling and testing in a controlled environment. LABflow was designed to replicate the real procedure that students would encounter in the field. The system allows students to register blood samples by entering patient information and selecting the tests that need to be performed. Once the sample is registered, printable labels are generated for the test tubes. After performing the tests, students return to the system to enter the test results. Finally, the system generates a professional-looking result PDF, just like the reports they would produce in a real-world lab setting. This provides a hands-on learning experience without the costs of commercial software.

Why we chose a loosely coupled tech stack:

We decided to build LABflow using a loosely coupled tech stack with Svelte for the frontend, Java Spring for the backend, and SQLite for the database. This approach gave us the flexibility to separate the front-end and back-end, which allowed us to design the system in a way that could be easily expanded or modified in the future. If we needed to change or update one part of the system (e.g., a complete rewrite of the backend or frontend), the other parts of the application would remain unaffected.

What I did:

In the early stages of the project, I focused heavily on the design of the application, ensuring that the user interface was intuitive and streamlined for the students. Later, I worked on the backend, focusing on creating the CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, Delete) that would allow users to register samples and tests, as well as manage the entire flow of information. My final contribution involved integrating the functionality for printing labels and registering test results directly within the system. This integration was crucial, as it allowed students to print real-world labels for their test tubes, which added an authentic touch to the learning experience.

Why SQLite was chosen:

We opted for SQLite as the database solution due to its lightweight nature and simplicity. Since the database would not need to store large amounts of data, SQLite provided an efficient solution that didn't require the overhead of managing a separate database service. We could simply save the SQL file for persistent storage, which simplified deployment and maintenance.

Outcome:

We are currently rolling out the first beta version of LABflow, which will be used in the second semester of the 2024-2025 school year. This version will allow students to start using the system for their blood sample tracking and test result generation.

Reflection:

While we haven't received official feedback yet, our clients (the teachers) were thrilled with the progress we made and expressed their appreciation multiple times. It's rare that proof of concept projects like this reach the hands of real users, so it has been incredibly rewarding to see the system being used by students in a real-world setting. We're excited to see how the system will evolve and impact the students' learning experience in the coming semesters.

projects.title: Thomas More Guide
projects.text:
Problem:

The Thomas More Geel campus is quite large and can be difficult to navigate, especially for new students or visitors. The goal of this project was to create an innovative application that not only provides a way to navigate the campus but also educates users about key spots, making the campus more accessible and engaging for newcomers.

How it was solved:

The Thomas More Guide app features a map of the campus with icons marking significant locations. Users can select a spot on the map and, using their smartphones, scan a QR code or image placed at that location. Once scanned, an Augmented Reality (AR) guide appears to provide information about the place. The guide explains interesting facts, history, or details about the location, creating a dynamic, self-guided tour experience.

The app was designed with non-technical users in mind, ensuring that anyone—regardless of technical expertise—could easily navigate the campus using just the map and the simple process of scanning an image. The goal was to make the app intuitive and user-friendly for everyone.

Your Role:

I started this project at the end of my second year and became the project lead, managing communication with the teachers who were our clients. My responsibilities included UX/UI design, ensuring the app was easy to navigate, as well as developing the Flutter application. Additionally, I contributed to the AR integration of the app. After I moved on from the project, it was continued by one of the newer Digital Innovation students.

Tech Details:

The app was developed using Flutter for cross-platform functionality, and the core AR feature was powered by Vuforia, an AR engine integrated with Unity. We used Vuforia's image tracking feature to trigger the AR guide when users scanned a specific picture or icon at various locations around the campus. This technology allowed us to create an interactive experience that could be used on regular smartphones.

Outcome:

The Proof of Concept (PoC) is still in development. I concluded my involvement with a successful demo where a phone scanned an image, and a virtual guide appeared, explaining details about the campus cafeteria. The next steps for the app include adding features like multi-language support and expanding the tour to cover more locations across the campus.

projects.title: Grow More
projects.text:
Problem:

The client, a company that runs a website offering games for people with disabilities, wanted a new, simple game that could be played by children with various limitations. The game needed to be very accessible, with constraints such as the absence of complex movements and the ability to play with mouse clicks or arrow keys only. The challenge was to create a game that would be engaging yet simple enough for people with disabilities, while still providing value and entertainment.

How Solved:

Grow More was designed with accessibility at its core. The gameplay involved a straightforward mechanic where players clicked on plants to make them grow. If using a mouse wasn't possible or too difficult, the game allowed players to use the spacebar as an alternative. The user's task was to grow plants in an empty room by clicking them (or using the spacebar), with each plant requiring more clicks to grow as the game progressed. Once the room was filled with fully grown plants, the game was complete.

The game was developed using Godot, an open-source game engine. The simplicity of Godot's system made it easy to develop the game's core mechanics and export it to a web-compatible format. The game's design was optimized for ease of use, making it accessible to everyone, regardless of their skill level.

What:

As the core gameplay mechanic, I focused on creating the plant growth system using Godot scripts to handle different plant growth stages. Each stage of a plant's growth was controlled by a unique sprite, with a progress bar indicating the growth. Once a plant reached full growth, the player could click on another plant to start the process again. The game became progressively harder, as each new plant required more clicks to fully grow.

Toon, my project partner, focused on the visual elements, including the game's menu system, graphical assets, and the overall look and feel of the game. Together, we ensured that the game was not only simple but also visually appealing for the target audience.

Technology Stack:

Godot (Game Engine)
GitHub/Git (Version control)
Web Export (For easy access and distribution via the website)

Outcome:

The final result was a simple, enjoyable game that was made available on the client's website for real users to play. Grow More became part of the broader portfolio of games for children with disabilities, offering a fun and accessible gaming experience.

Process:

This project was our first experience working within the Digital Innovation program, so we adhered to the Scrum methodology to organize our work. This included using Trello to track tasks, holding daily stand-ups, and conducting sprint retrospectives. While the agile approach proved valuable, especially for larger teams, it felt a bit cumbersome for a two-person project. However, it provided a solid foundation for how we approached our work, managed tasks, and improved over the course of the project.

projects.title: SignalGuard - project 4.0
projects.text:
Problem:

SignalGuard was a collaborative project developed by students from different IT specializations, including Application Development, AI & Data Visualization, Cloud & Cybersecurity, and Digital Innovation. The project was built for Cipal Schaubroeck, a company that specializes in ANPR camera systems for traffic monitoring. Since these cameras were a relatively new addition to their product line, Cipal needed a monitoring system to help both their technicians and clients identify and resolve issues faster.

Understanding the Problem:

Our project focused on solving three major challenges:

  • Remote Power Cycling: Many ANPR camera issues could be resolved simply by powering the system off and on again, yet technicians still had to be sent on-site to do this manually. We aimed to create a solution that would allow remote resets with the press of a button.
  • Automated Alert Prioritization: The system generated an overwhelming number of error messages and status updates every hour. These alerts had to be filtered manually, which was inefficient. We sought to automate the prioritization of these messages, ensuring that only the most critical issues required immediate attention.
  • Last Line of Communication: When a complete system failure occurred, there was no fallback method of communication. This meant that technicians were sent in blindly, increasing the risk of delayed repairs and putting Cipal at risk of breaching Service Level Agreements (SLAs) with their clients.

Project Roles & Collaboration:

Each specialization within our team focused on a different part of the system:

  • Application Development students and I worked on building the frontend and backend of the application.
  • The AI & Data Visualization student analyzed system data and worked on automated alert prioritization.
  • The Cloud & Cybersecurity student ensured that the system was securely hosted and deployed online.
  • As a Digital Innovation student, I took on the role of project manager, leading the daily scrum meetings and ensuring effective collaboration between all team members.

Technical Approach & Implementation:

For the frontend, we used React, while the backend was built using Fastify, a modern web framework for Node.js that outperforms ExpressJS in terms of speed and efficiency. We chose PostgreSQL as our database and integrated Prisma ORM for secure and optimized SQL operations.

On the hardware side, we deployed an OrangePI mini-computer inside the ANPR camera system’s electrical box. This allowed us to monitor power levels and breaker switches, ensuring that power loss issues could be detected remotely. We also installed a relay board, which allowed us to remotely cut and restore power to critical components, such as the internet modem.

Due to the tight three-week development timeline, we focused on building a proof of concept (PoC) with core functionality. Unfortunately, we did not have enough time to implement real-time data processing or full logging capabilities.

Challenges & Limitations:

  • Learning Curve with Fastify: Fastify provided performance benefits over older frameworks, but its lack of documentation made it difficult to work with at times.
  • Lack of Quality Data for AI: We initially planned to integrate AI-driven issue detection, but the available data was too unstructured to train a reliable model. As a result, AI features were ultimately scrapped from the project.
  • Time Constraints: With only three sprints (one week each) to develop the project, we had to prioritize essential features. This meant that advanced functionalities, such as real-time monitoring and data visualization, had to be left out.

My Contributions & Learning Experience:

In addition to leading project management efforts, I personally developed the JWT-based authentication system for the frontend and backend, including full role-based access control. I also helped with feature planning and UI design, ensuring that the application included:

  • A map-based interface displaying all ANPR camera locations
  • A notification dashboard for tracking alerts
  • A client management system

Even though the AI component was not implemented, I was actively involved in researching possible AI integrations and learned a lot about data structuring and analysis during the process.

Project Outcome & Future Potential:

The final product was delivered to Cipal Schaubroeck as a Proof of Concept (PoC). While the company is unlikely to use our exact implementation, our work laid the foundation for their future monitoring system. Certain features—like remote power cycling—could potentially be integrated into their production systems, helping reduce maintenance costs and improve response times.

Even though this project had its limitations, it was a valuable learning experience, showing me the importance of collaborating with different IT disciplines, prioritizing tasks under time pressure, and adapting to unexpected challenges.

projects.title: BPMN Bn Log 29
projects.text:
Problem:

During my studies at the Thomas More University of Applied Sciences, we were assigned a project to develop a Business Process Model Notation (BPMN) for an organization. This required us to collaborate with a company and visualize one of their internal processes. Thanks to my teammate Toon, who was already in the military, we had the unique opportunity to work with the 29th Logistics Battalion in Grobbendonk. This allowed us to model a process that wasn't something typically covered in business studies—making it an exciting challenge. We focused on their transportation request process, covering everything from the initial request for transporting goods to the final completion of the task.

How it was solved:

Together with three fellow students, we were invited to spend a day at their barracks to gain firsthand insights into their workflow. The visit started with a tour of the facility, where we observed their logistical operations in action. Afterward, we conducted an in-depth interview with 1Lt De Dapper, who explained how transportation requests were handled. This step was essential in understanding the key decision points and ensuring that our model accurately reflected the real-world process.

The following day, our team spent the entire day working together to construct a detailed BPMN diagram. Since this was our first time working with BPMN, it was a learning experience for all of us. One of the biggest challenges we faced was translating military acronyms into a clear and understandable process. The personnel at the barracks were so accustomed to using these terms that it was sometimes difficult for us to follow. Fortunately, Toon had experience working there and was able to help bridge the gap whenever we struggled with unfamiliar terminology.

Outcome:

Once we completed the BPMN diagram, we contacted our professor to schedule a presentation of our findings. This final step was crucial, as it allowed us to showcase our ability to analyze a real-world process and translate it into a structured business model. Our presentation highlighted the importance of BPMN in identifying inefficiencies and optimizing business operations.

Reflection:

This project was a valuable learning experience in business process modeling and collaboration with an external organization. It was fascinating to see how logistics are arranged within the Belgian military, and it gave us a deeper appreciation for how structured processes contribute to efficiency. Additionally, the experience reinforced the importance of teamwork, clear communication, and structured analysis—skills that will undoubtedly be useful in future projects.

projects.title: PURplus planning app
projects.text:
Problem:

As a personal project, I built a custom agenda application for my parents' construction business to help them efficiently manage their scheduled jobs. The app was developed using PHP Laravel with a MySQL database to store and display job information.

How it was solved:

The goal was to create a simple and intuitive interface that showed crucial job details at a glance, reducing the need for manual scheduling and improving overall organization. Laravel’s framework made it easy to implement user authentication, job management, and database interactions, while MySQL ensured reliable data storage.

Outcome:

This project was a great opportunity to improve my backend development skills, work with database structuring, and gain experience in building practical business solutions.

projects.title: Blended Intensive Program
projects.text:
Concept:

Tijdens een intensieve week kregen we de kans om Tallinn en haar rol in innovatie en onderzoek van dichtbij te ontdekken. We leerden hoe we ideeën konden omzetten in tastbare resultaten, hoe we projecten effectief moesten pitchen en hoe we konden nagaan of er marktinteresse was, met een goed onderbouwd businessplan als uitgangspunt.

Our challenge:

Met het concept van een slimme en duurzame stad in gedachten, kregen we de opdracht om een tool te ontwikkelen die zowel in Tallinn als daarbuiten gebruikt kon worden. Gedurende de week werden we ondergedompeld in de innovaties die de stad te bieden heeft en volgden we workshops over marktonderzoek en het pitchen van ideeën aan investeerders.

Binnen onze groep brainstormden we over verschillende concepten en kwamen we uiteindelijk tot het idee om een applicatie te ontwikkelen die mensen op een sportieve manier met elkaar in contact brengt door sportevenementen te organiseren. Dit concept bood een interessante manier om sociale interactie te stimuleren en paste goed binnen het thema van een slimme en duurzame stad. Door de workshops en feedbacksessies kregen we de kans om het idee verder uit te werken en aan te scherpen.

We werkten aan dit project voor de Entrepreneurship University of Applied Sciences, gevestigd in Ülemiste City, een business center net buiten het centrum van Tallinn. Dit gebied is een broedplaats voor innovatie en trekt veel internationale bedrijven en professionals aan. Hierdoor kregen we niet alleen inzichten van docenten, maar ook van ondernemers en andere experts die dagelijks met innovatie en marktvalidatie bezig zijn.

Outcome:

Deze ervaring gaf me waardevolle inzichten in ondernemerschap, innovatie en hoe je een idee effectief aan de markt presenteert. Het was inspirerend om in een omgeving te werken waar vernieuwing centraal staat en om te leren hoe je een concept omvormt tot een levensvatbaar project.
